Hilbert Functions and Line Bundle Cohomology on CICY Threefolds

Juntao Wang Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Beijing 101408, China Email: jtwang.bimsa@gmail.com
Abstract

Line bundle cohomology on complete intersection Calabi–Yau threefolds is an important input in string phenomenology. Previous work, based on direct extrapolation and on machine-learning analyses of finite data sets, has shown that these cohomology dimensions often admit chamber-wise polynomial descriptions on the Picard lattice. In this paper we explain this structure through the Hilbert functions associated with the non-trivial maps in the Koszul spectral sequence. Once Bott–Borel–Weil theory determines the non-vanishing ambient cohomology groups, the rank defects of the relevant Koszul maps are governed by Hilbert functions of cokernel or kernel modules. This turns many empirical chamber formulae into explicit rank-defect statements, with proofs that are either analytic or certified on finite boxes. Using this approach, we recover analytically almost all of the piecewise formulae appearing in the existing literature. For the remaining cases, we prove finite-box certificate theorems for infinite families of line bundles in the specified regions. We also identify new wall structures on certain CICYs which refine the chamber decompositions suggested by finite-range data. Finally, we use the same framework to construct line bundle cohomology formula libraries for two CICY threefolds which had not previously been analysed in this way. These results suggest that Hilbert-function methods can provide promising faster inputs for future string model-building scans based on line bundle constructions.

Keywords
Calabi–Yau manifolds, sheaf cohomology, Hilbert functions, string model building

1 Introduction

Line bundle and bundle-valued cohomology are basic inputs in string model building. For example, in heterotic compactifications, they determine spectra, vector-like matter, singlets and many other physics quantities. They are needed in large-scale scans of monad bundle models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and line bundle sum models on complete intersection Calabi–Yau threefolds in products of projective spaces (CICYs) [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], toric hypersurfaces [13], elliptically fibered Calabi–Yau threefolds [14], and generalized CICYs [15, 16]. Line-bundle cohomology also appears in related model-building problems, including Yukawa and spectral questions and many other questions [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

The practical importance of these computations has led to dedicated software and search strategies. Existing CICY computations for monad model-building and line-bundle sum model-building use Koszul-sequence methods developed in the early algorithmic heterotic literature cited above, while cohomCalg implements methods for line-bundle cohomology on toric Calabi–Yau manifolds [22, 23]. More recent model-building searches use reinforcement learning, genetic algorithms, and quantum annealing to navigate large spaces of line-bundle or monad data [24, 25, 26, 27]. These developments make the same bottleneck increasingly visible: one must evaluate many cohomology dimensions, often for large families of line bundles, and the expensive part is usually the rank of the induced Koszul maps.

For CICYs, the standard calculation resolves 𝒪X​(k)\mathcal{O}_{X}(k) by the ambient Koszul complex, computes ambient cohomology by the Bott–Borel–Weil theorem and the Künneth formula, and then determines the ranks of the maps induced by the defining equations [28, 29]. The ambient dimensions are explicit binomial expressions, but the induced maps are often large and their ranks vary with the line-bundle vector kk. Direct rank computation is reliable, but it can become expensive in many cases, making systematic scans very time consuming.

Several recent studies have approached this bottleneck from different directions, and substantial evidence has been gathered that these ranks are highly structured. Chamber-wise formulae were found for several CICYs in [30], and for favourable codimension-two CICYs in [31]. It was also shown that line-bundle cohomology formulae can be reconstructed from finite data by machine-learning methods [32, 33]. Line-bundle cohomology under flops and across extended Kahler cones was studied in [34]. In [35], line-bundle cohomology generating functions are constructed from Hilbert–Poincare series associated with coordinate rings and Cox rings; see also [36] for recent developments in line-bundle cohomology and applications to string phenomenology. The common outcome is that line-bundle cohomology is often governed by piecewise polynomial formulae.

Empirically, the main phenomenon is therefore the appearance of piecewise chamber structures with Hilbert-function-like behaviour in the line-bundle variables. These chambers are polynomial in nature, but they are separated by walls where additional corrections appear and where naive maximal-rank expectations fail. Some of these walls are already forced by the Bott–Borel–Weil decomposition of the ambient cohomology groups, while others are not visible from the ambient cohomology data alone.

The point of this paper is to explain this phenomenon from the perspective of Hilbert functions. After Bott–Borel–Weil identifies the nonzero ambient cohomology rows, Serre duality converts top cohomology into dual polynomial pieces. The relevant Koszul differential then becomes a homogeneous map of graded or multigraded modules over a polynomial ring in the remaining variables,

Φ:⨁jR⁡(−αj)⟶⨁ℓR⁡(−βℓ).\Phi:\bigoplus_{j}R(-\alpha_{j})\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{\ell}R(-\beta_{\ell}). (1)

For a fixed line bundle, the matrix appearing in the CICY computation is the degree b=b⁡(k)b=b(k) component Φb\Phi_{b}. Hence, if M=coker⁡ΦM=\coker\Phi, then

dimcoker⁡(Φb)=HF⁡(M,b),rank⁡(Φb)=dim(⨁ℓRb−βℓ)−HF⁡(M,b).\dim\coker(\Phi_{b})=\operatorname{HF}(M,b),\qquad\rank(\Phi_{b})=\dim\!\left(\bigoplus_{\ell}R_{b-\beta_{\ell}}\right)-\operatorname{HF}(M,b). (2)

The same dictionary applies to endpoint maps, where kernel Hilbert functions appear instead of cokernel Hilbert functions. In this way, chamber formulae on the Picard lattice can be interpreted as Hilbert functions of remaining modules evaluated along degrees depending affinely on kk.

This viewpoint explains several structural features of known formulae. A free resolution of the graded module determines a Hilbert series whose numerator encodes the syzygies responsible for rank defects. Extracting coefficients then produces the piecewise polynomial contributions and gives an algebraic explanation for their wall behaviour. A key advantage is that the kernel or cokernel is treated as a graded module, so its Hilbert series encodes all degrees at once and therefore controls infinitely many line bundles. This often reveals structures which are difficult to see from finite-box formula extrapolation alone; several such refinements appear below.

Analytic minimal resolutions of the residual graded modules are still difficult to obtain in many cases. However, the Hilbert numerator can also be certified by Gröbner-basis computations or by rank certificates for finitely many matrices, without losing the cohomological information needed here. This gives theorem-level finite-box statements on specified regions, often leaving some coordinates free and hence covering infinitely many line bundles. These computations also indicate where further analytic structure should emerge.

From a computational perspective, a certified Hilbert function replaces large families of Koszul rank computations. Once the graded module is understood, cohomology in the corresponding chamber is obtained by coefficient extraction or closed formulae. This provides a practical route toward efficient line-bundle cohomology libraries for CICYs and, potentially, for related toric Calabi–Yau threefolds and their freely acting quotients.

The results of this paper are as follows. First, we recover analytically almost all of the known chamber formulae treated here by identifying the corresponding Hilbert functions in the remaining variables. Second, the Hilbert numerators reveal additional structures not visible from source–target dimensions or finite-range polynomial fitting, including hidden subwalls inside fixed ambient-cohomology regions and delayed wall contributions beyond naive maximal-rank expectations. Third, we obtain new line-bundle cohomology formulae for CICY examples not previously treated in this framework, combining analytic Hilbert-series methods with replayable finite-box certificates.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces the Koszul spectral sequence for line bundles and explains the Hilbert-function rank-defect dictionary. Section 3 applies this dictionary to known hypersurface and codimension-two formulae. Section 4 presents new wall structures and new formula packages. The appendices contain the technical reductions, exactness statements, and certificate formats used in the finite-box arguments.

2 From CICY Koszul maps to Hilbert functions

Line bundle cohomology on a CICY is computed via the Koszul resolution on the ambient space. After the Bott–Borel–Weil theorem determines which ambient cohomology groups are nonzero, the remaining task is to compute the ranks of the maps induced by the defining equations. In each degree, these maps are graded components of homogeneous maps between graded modules over the Cox ring of the ambient space. Their rank defects in a given degree are therefore given by the value of the Hilbert function of the corresponding cokernel module in that degree. This observation links the Koszul spectral sequence to the chamber-by-chamber formulae for Hilbert functions studied below.

2.1 The Koszul spectral sequence

Let

A=∏i=1mℙniA=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}^{n_{i}} (3)

and let X⊂AX\subset A be a smooth complete intersection cut out by a regular sequence

f1,…,fc,deg⁡(fα)=dα∈ℤm.f_{1},\ldots,f_{c},\qquad\deg(f_{\alpha})=d_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. (4)

XX is a CICY threefold when

dimX=∑ini−c=3,∑α=1cdα​i=ni+1for each factor ℙni.\dim X=\sum_{i}n_{i}-c=3,\quad\sum_{\alpha=1}^{c}d_{\alpha i}=n_{i}+1\quad\text{for each factor }\mathbb{P}^{n_{i}}.

For k=(k1,…,km)∈ℤmk=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}, write

𝒪X​(k)=𝒪A​(k)|X.\mathcal{O}_{X}(k)=\mathcal{O}_{A}(k)|_{X}.

The ambient Koszul resolution of this line bundle is

0→⋀cE∨⊗𝒪A​(k)→⋯→E∨⊗𝒪A​(k)→𝒪A​(k)→𝒪X​(k)→0,0\to\bigwedge^{c}E^{\vee}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{A}(k)\to\cdots\to E^{\vee}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{A}(k)\to\mathcal{O}_{A}(k)\to\mathcal{O}_{X}(k)\to 0, (5)

where

E=⨁α=1c𝒪A​(dα).E=\bigoplus_{\alpha=1}^{c}\mathcal{O}_{A}(d_{\alpha}). (6)

Equivalently, the pp-th Koszul term is

Kp​(k)=⨁I⊂{1,…,c}|I|=p𝒪A​(k−∑α∈Idα),0≤p≤c.K_{p}(k)=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset\{1,\ldots,c\}\\ |I|=p\end{subarray}}\mathcal{O}_{A}\Big(k-\sum_{\alpha\in I}d_{\alpha}\Big),\qquad 0\leq p\leq c. (7)

The differential Kp​(k)→Kp−1​(k)K_{p}(k)\to K_{p-1}(k) is the signed contraction with (f1,…,fc)(f_{1},\ldots,f_{c}).

Taking hypercohomology gives the standard Koszul spectral sequence

E1−p,q=Hq​(A,Kp​(k)),0≤p≤c,E_{1}^{-p,q}=H^{q}(A,K_{p}(k)),\qquad 0\leq p\leq c, (8)

E1−p,q=Hq​(A,Kp​(k))⟹Hq−p​(X,𝒪X​(k)).E_{1}^{-p,q}=H^{q}(A,K_{p}(k))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^{q-p}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(k)). (9)

The first differential is induced by the Koszul differential,

d1:E1−p,q⟶E1−p+1,q.d_{1}:E_{1}^{-p,q}\longrightarrow E_{1}^{-p+1,q}. (10)

More generally,

dr:Er−p,q⟶Er−p+r,q−r+1,d_{r}:E_{r}^{-p,q}\longrightarrow E_{r}^{-p+r,q-r+1}, (11)

and

Er+1−p,q=ker(dr:Er−p,q→Er−p+r,q−r+1)im(dr:Er−p−r,q+r−1→Er−p,q).E_{r+1}^{-p,q}=\frac{\ker\!\left(d_{r}:E_{r}^{-p,q}\to E_{r}^{-p+r,q-r+1}\right)}{\operatorname{im}\!\left(d_{r}:E_{r}^{-p-r,q+r-1}\to E_{r}^{-p,q}\right)}. (12)

Thus the higher differentials are not extra choices: they are the connecting maps forced by the same Koszul differential after the preceding kernels and images have been taken.

The stable page gives a filtration of Hi​(X,𝒪X​(k))H^{i}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(k)), with graded pieces E∞−p,i+pE_{\infty}^{-p,i+p}. In particular,

hi​(X,𝒪X​(k))=∑pdimE∞−p,i+p.h^{i}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(k))=\sum_{p}\dim E_{\infty}^{-p,i+p}. (13)

Consequently, computing line bundle cohomology separates into two parts: first determining the ambient groups Hq​(A,Kp​(k))H^{q}(A,K_{p}(k)), and then determining the ranks of the differentials between them.

The first part is explicit. On a projective factor ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, Bott–Borel–Weil gives

Hj​(ℙn,𝒪ℙn​(a))≠0H^{j}(\mathbb{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}(a))\neq 0 (14)

only in the following cases:

range of ​anonzero cohomologydimensiona≥0H0(a+nn)−n≤a≤−1none0a≤−n−1Hn(−a−1n).\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\text{range of }a&\text{nonzero cohomology}&\text{dimension}\\ \hline\cr a\geq 0&H^{0}&\binom{a+n}{n}\\ -n\leq a\leq-1&\text{none}&0\\ a\leq-n-1&H^{n}&\binom{-a-1}{n}.\end{array} (15)

By the Künneth formula, the cohomology of a line bundle on AA is the tensor product of the corresponding factorwise cohomology groups. As kk varies, the inequalities in (15) divide the Picard lattice into corresponding ambient-cohomology regions.

Inside one such region, every nonzero ambient group is a tensor product of polynomial spaces and dual polynomial spaces. We use

H0​(ℙn,𝒪⁡(a))≃ℂ​[x0,…,xn]a(a≥0),H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}(a))\simeq\mathbb{C}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}]_{a}\qquad(a\geq 0),

and, by Serre duality,

Hn​(ℙn,𝒪⁡(−a−n−1))∨≃ℂ​[x0,…,xn]a(a≥0).H^{n}(\mathbb{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}(-a-n-1))^{\vee}\simeq\mathbb{C}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}]_{a}\qquad(a\geq 0).

After choosing monomial bases, the maps between nonzero ambient groups become concrete polynomial multiplication maps induced by the defining equations fαf_{\alpha}. The dimensions of kernels and cokernels of these maps are the nontrivial input in the cohomology calculation.

2.2 A concrete codimension-two example with a d2d_{2} map

We next recall a simple example in which a higher differential can be written explicitly as a multiplication map. Consider the codimension-two CICY

X=[ℙx111ℙy423]⊂A=ℙx1×ℙy4.X=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|cc}\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}&1&1\\ \mathbb{P}^{4}_{y}&2&3\end{array}\right]\subset A=\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}\times\mathbb{P}^{4}_{y}. (16)

F=x0​f0​(y)+x1​f1​(y),G=x0​g0​(y)+x1​g1​(y),F=x_{0}f_{0}(y)+x_{1}f_{1}(y),\qquad G=x_{0}g_{0}(y)+x_{1}g_{1}(y), (17)

E10,0\displaystyle E_{1}^{0,0} =H0​(A,K0)≃H0​(ℙ4,𝒪⁡(b)),\displaystyle=H^{0}(A,K_{0})\simeq H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{4},\mathcal{O}(b)), (19)
E1−2,1\displaystyle E_{1}^{-2,1} =H1​(A,K2)≃H1​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(−2))⊗H0​(ℙ4,𝒪⁡(b−5)).\displaystyle=H^{1}(A,K_{2})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(-2))\otimes H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{4},\mathcal{O}(b-5)). (20)

R=ℂ⁡[y0,…,y4],R=\mathbb{C}[y_{0},\ldots,y_{4}],

2.3 Graded modules and rank defects

We now formulate the preceding observation in the language used in the rest of the paper. Let RR be the Cox ring of the ambient space. For a single projective space this is just

R=ℂ⁡[z0,…,zn],deg⁡zμ=1,R=\mathbb{C}[z_{0},\ldots,z_{n}],\qquad\deg z_{\mu}=1,

with Rd≃H0​(ℙn,𝒪⁡(d))R_{d}\simeq H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}(d)). For a product of projective spaces it is multigraded:

R=ℂ[zi,μ∣1≤i≤s, 0≤μ≤ni],degzi,μ=ei∈ℤs,R=\mathbb{C}[z_{i,\mu}\mid 1\leq i\leq s,\ 0\leq\mu\leq n_{i}],\qquad\deg z_{i,\mu}=e_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}^{s},

and

R(d1,…,ds)≅H0(ℙn1×⋯×ℙns,𝒪(d1,…,ds))R_{(d_{1},\ldots,d_{s})}\cong H^{0}\!\left(\mathbb{P}^{n_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{P}^{n_{s}},\mathcal{O}(d_{1},\ldots,d_{s})\right)

whenever all di≥0d_{i}\geq 0.

Inside a fixed ambient-cohomology region, the relevant Koszul differential is a degree piece of a homogeneous map

Φ:F=⨁aR⁡(−αa)⟶G=⨁ℓR⁡(−βℓ).\Phi:F=\bigoplus_{a}R(-\alpha_{a})\longrightarrow G=\bigoplus_{\ell}R(-\beta_{\ell}). (30)

For a given line bundle kk, the actual finite-dimensional matrix is the degree 𝐛=𝐛⁡(k)\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}(k) piece

Φ𝐛:F𝐛⟶G𝐛.\Phi_{\mathbf{b}}:F_{\mathbf{b}}\longrightarrow G_{\mathbf{b}}. (31)

Here 𝐛⁡(k)\mathbf{b}(k) is an affine function of the line bundle parameters in the chamber. If

M=coker⁡Φ,M=\coker\Phi,

then MM is a graded RR-module and

M𝐛=G𝐛/Φ𝐛​(F𝐛)=coker⁡(Φ𝐛).M_{\mathbf{b}}=G_{\mathbf{b}}/\Phi_{\mathbf{b}}(F_{\mathbf{b}})=\coker(\Phi_{\mathbf{b}}).

Its Hilbert function is

HF⁡(M,𝐛)=dimℂM𝐛.\operatorname{HF}(M,\mathbf{b})=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}M_{\mathbf{b}}. (32)

Therefore

rank⁡Φ𝐛=dimG𝐛−HF⁡(M,𝐛).\rank\Phi_{\mathbf{b}}=\dim G_{\mathbf{b}}-\operatorname{HF}(M,\mathbf{b}). (33)

This is the rank-defect principle. The failure of the matrix Φ𝐛\Phi_{\mathbf{b}} to have full target rank is measured by the Hilbert function of one fixed graded module. Kernels are obtained from the same identity:

dimker⁡Φ𝐛=dimF𝐛−dimG𝐛+HF⁡(M,𝐛).\dim\ker\Phi_{\mathbf{b}}=\dim F_{\mathbf{b}}-\dim G_{\mathbf{b}}+\operatorname{HF}(M,\mathbf{b}). (34)

Thus every kernel or cokernel contribution in the Koszul spectral sequence can be expressed in terms of Hilbert functions of graded modules in the remaining variables.

A free resolution packages these Hilbert functions uniformly. Suppose

0→Fs→Fs−1→⋯→F1→F0→M→0,Fi=⨁jR⁡(−γi​j).0\to F_{s}\to F_{s-1}\to\cdots\to F_{1}\to F_{0}\to M\to 0,\qquad F_{i}=\bigoplus_{j}R(-\gamma_{ij}). (35)

Then additivity of dimensions in each degree gives

HS⁡(M;𝐭)=HS⁡(R;𝐭)​∑i(−1)i​∑j𝐭γi​j.\operatorname{HS}(M;\mathbf{t})=\operatorname{HS}(R;\mathbf{t})\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\sum_{j}\mathbf{t}^{\gamma_{ij}}. (36)

The polynomial

NM​(𝐭)=∑i(−1)i​∑j𝐭γi​jN_{M}(\mathbf{t})=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\sum_{j}\mathbf{t}^{\gamma_{ij}} (37)

is the Hilbert numerator. Once NMN_{M} is known, the required dimensions are obtained by coefficient extraction from HS⁡(M,𝐭)\operatorname{HS}(M;\mathbf{t}).

In computations it is often unnecessary, and sometimes impractical, to display a full minimal free resolution. It is enough to certify the Hilbert function or Hilbert numerator. One standard route is to compute an initial module: after a term order has been fixed, Gröbner degeneration preserves Hilbert functions. If in⁡(M)\operatorname{in}(M) denotes the monomial module defined by the leading terms of a Gröbner basis for the presentation of MM, then

HF⁡(M,𝐛)=HF⁡(in⁡(M),𝐛).\operatorname{HF}(M,\mathbf{b})=\operatorname{HF}(\operatorname{in}(M),\mathbf{b}).

This is the computational commutative-algebra form of the rank-defect principle used in the finite-box certificates below.

The example of the previous subsection corresponds to

M=R/(Δ).M=R/(\Delta).

Indeed,

Mb=(R/(Δ))b=Rb/Δ​Rb−5,M_{b}=(R/(\Delta))_{b}=R_{b}/\Delta R_{b-5}, (38)

and hence

h0​(X,𝒪X​(0,b))=HF⁡(R/(Δ),b).h^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(0,b))=\operatorname{HF}(R/(\Delta),b). (39)

The free resolution

0⟶R⁡(−5)⟶⋅ΔR⟶R/(Δ)⟶00\longrightarrow R(-5)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot\Delta}}{{\longrightarrow}}R\longrightarrow R/(\Delta)\longrightarrow 0 (40)

gives

HS⁡(R/(Δ),t)=1−t5(1−t)5.\operatorname{HS}(R/(\Delta);t)=\frac{1-t^{5}}{(1-t)^{5}}. (41)

Extracting the coefficient of tbt^{b} recovers

HF⁡(R/(Δ),b)=(b+44)−(b−14),\operatorname{HF}(R/(\Delta),b)=\binom{b+4}{4}-\binom{b-1}{4}, (42)

with the convention that Rb−5=0R_{b-5}=0 for b<5b<5. This is the simplest instance of a chamber formula arising from a Hilbert function.

2.4 Elementary rank-defect models

We finish with three small algebraic models. They are not meant as new results; their role is to fix the notation and to illustrate the types of graded modules which occur later.

One equation.

Let

R=ℂ⁡[z0,…,zn],R=\mathbb{C}[z_{0},\ldots,z_{n}],

and let H∈RdH\in R_{d} be a nonzero homogeneous polynomial. At degree bb, multiplication by HH gives

μb:Rb−d⟶Rb,u⟼u​H.\mu_{b}:R_{b-d}\longrightarrow R_{b},\qquad u\longmapsto uH. (43)

The rank defect is

DH​(b):=dimcoker⁡μb=dimRb−rank⁡μb.D_{H}(b):=\dim\coker\mu_{b}=\dim R_{b}-\rank\mu_{b}. (44)

Since RR is a domain, μb\mu_{b} is injective whenever Rb−d≠0R_{b-d}\neq 0. Thus

DH​(b)=(b+nn)−(b−d+nn),D_{H}(b)=\binom{b+n}{n}-\binom{b-d+n}{n}, (45)

where the second term is omitted when b<db<d. Equivalently,

coker⁡μb=(R/(H))b,\coker\mu_{b}=(R/(H))_{b},

and

0⟶R⁡(−d)⟶⋅HR⟶R/(H)⟶00\longrightarrow R(-d)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\cdot H}}{{\longrightarrow}}R\longrightarrow R/(H)\longrightarrow 0 (46)

gives

HS⁡(R/(H);t)=1−td(1−t)n+1,HF⁡(R/(H),b)=(b+nn)−(b−d+nn).\operatorname{HS}(R/(H);t)=\frac{1-t^{d}}{(1-t)^{n+1}},\qquad\operatorname{HF}(R/(H),b)=\binom{b+n}{n}-\binom{b-d+n}{n}. (47)
A scalar complete intersection.

Let

R=ℂ⁡[x0,x1,x2],R=\mathbb{C}[x_{0},x_{1},x_{2}],

and let A,B∈R2A,B\in R_{2} be two generic quadrics. Consider

Φb:Rb−2⊕2⟶Rb,(u,v)⟼u​A+v​B.\Phi_{b}:R_{b-2}^{\oplus 2}\longrightarrow R_{b},\qquad(u,v)\longmapsto uA+vB. (48)

The image is the degree-bb part of the ideal (A,B)(A,B), so

coker⁡Φb=(R/(A,B))b.\coker\Phi_{b}=(R/(A,B))_{b}.

Since A,BA,B form a regular sequence, the Koszul resolution is

0⟶R⁡(−4)⟶R​(−2)2⟶(A​B)R⟶R/(A,B)⟶0.0\longrightarrow R(-4)\longrightarrow R(-2)^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(A\ B)}}{{\longrightarrow}}R\longrightarrow R/(A,B)\longrightarrow 0. (49)

Hence

HS⁡(R/(A,B);t)=(1−t2)2(1−t)3,\operatorname{HS}(R/(A,B);t)=\frac{(1-t^{2})^{2}}{(1-t)^{3}}, (50)

and

HF⁡(R/(A,B),b)=(b+22)−2​(b2)+(b−22).\operatorname{HF}(R/(A,B),b)=\binom{b+2}{2}-2\binom{b}{2}+\binom{b-2}{2}. (51)

Thus

rank⁡Φb=(b+22)−HF⁡(R/(A,B),b).\rank\Phi_{b}=\binom{b+2}{2}-\operatorname{HF}(R/(A,B),b).

For b≥4b\geq 4, the Hilbert function is the constant 44, the length of the complete intersection of two quadrics in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}. The appearance of the final term in (51) is already a simple example of a chamber wall in degree.

A vector-valued cokernel.

Finally, active maps need not have scalar targets. Let

R=ℂ⁡[x,y,z],R=\mathbb{C}[x,y,z],

and consider

Φ:R​(−1)3⟶R2,(u,v,w)⟼(x​u+y​v,x​v+y​w).\Phi:R(-1)^{3}\longrightarrow R^{2},\qquad(u,v,w)\longmapsto(xu+yv,\;xv+yw). (52)

Equivalently,

Φ=(xy00xy).\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}x&y&0\\ 0&x&y\end{pmatrix}.

At degree bb this gives

Φb:Rb−1⊕3⟶Rb⊕2.\Phi_{b}:R_{b-1}^{\oplus 3}\longrightarrow R_{b}^{\oplus 2}.

The cokernel is a genuine module M=coker⁡ΦM=\coker\Phi, not a quotient ring R/IR/I. The kernel of Φ\Phi is generated by

(y2,−x​y,x2),(y^{2},-xy,x^{2}),

and hence

0⟶R⁡(−3)⟶(y2,−x​y,x2)R​(−1)3⟶ΦR2⟶M⟶0.0\longrightarrow R(-3)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(y^{2},-xy,x^{2})}}{{\longrightarrow}}R(-1)^{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}R^{2}\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0. (53)

Therefore

HS⁡(M,t)=2−3​t+t3(1−t)3,\operatorname{HS}(M;t)=\frac{2-3t+t^{3}}{(1-t)^{3}}, (54)

so

HF⁡(M,b)=2​(b+22)−3​(b+12)+(b−12).\operatorname{HF}(M,b)=2\binom{b+2}{2}-3\binom{b+1}{2}+\binom{b-1}{2}. (55)

Consequently,

rank⁡Φb=dimRb⊕2−HF⁡(M,b).\rank\Phi_{b}=\dim R_{b}^{\oplus 2}-\operatorname{HF}(M,b).

This is the prototype for the vector-valued active maps appearing later: the rank defect is still a Hilbert function, but the relevant object is a cokernel module rather than a scalar quotient ring.

3 From Hilbert functions to line bundle cohomology

In this section, we apply the mechanism explained in the last section to examples studied in the literature. We will recover most of their formula analytically and put those where new structure pops up in the next section. We will first discuss the hypersurface CICYs and then the codimension two cases.

3.1 Hypersurface formulae

The hypersurface examples are the cleanest testing ground for the method in this paper, because the Koszul resolution has at most one nontrivial multiplication map. Nevertheless, they already display non-trivial relationships between rank phenomena and Hilbert funcitons. We first treat the ℙ1×ℙn\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{n} family as the model calculation; then we discuss the bicubic and two multigraded hypersurface examples.

3.1.1 ℙ1×ℙn\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{n} hypersurfaces

Let

X={f=0}⊂ℙx1×ℙynX=\{f=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}\times\mathbb{P}^{n}_{y}

be a smooth hypersurface of bidegree (d,e)(d,e), and write

f=∑i=0dx0d−i​x1i​fi​(y),fi∈Se,S=ℂ⁡[y0,…,yn].f=\sum_{i=0}^{d}x_{0}^{d-i}x_{1}^{i}f_{i}(y),\qquad f_{i}\in S_{e},\qquad S=\mathbb{C}[y_{0},\ldots,y_{n}].

0⟶𝒪ℙ1×ℙn​(−r−d,b−e)→𝑓𝒪ℙ1×ℙn​(−r,b)⟶𝒪X​(−r,b)⟶00\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{n}}(-r-d,b-e)\xrightarrow{\ f\ }\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{n}}(-r,b)\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,b)\longrightarrow 0

On this cohomology row, the map induced by multiplication by ff, after Serre duality on the ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-factor, becomes a graded map over SS.

Choose the monomial bases

H1​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(−r−d))≃H0​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(r+d−2))∨,H1​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(−r))≃H0​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(r−2))∨.H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(-r-d))\simeq H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(r+d-2))^{\vee},\qquad H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(-r))\simeq H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(r-2))^{\vee}.

Contraction by ∑x0d−i​x1i​fi\sum x_{0}^{d-i}x_{1}^{i}f_{i} gives the map

Φr:S​(−e)r+d−1⟶Sr−1.\Phi_{r}:S(-e)^{r+d-1}\longrightarrow S^{r-1}.

With respect to the ordered monomial bases, this map is represented by the matrix

Sylr,d⁡(f0,…,fd)=(f0f1⋯fd0⋯00f0f1⋯fd⋱⋱⋱⋱⋱00⋯0f0f1⋯fd),\operatorname{Syl}_{r,d}(f_{0},\ldots,f_{d})=\begin{pmatrix}f_{0}&f_{1}&\cdots&f_{d}&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&f_{0}&f_{1}&\cdots&f_{d}&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots&0\\ 0&\cdots&0&f_{0}&f_{1}&\cdots&f_{d}\end{pmatrix}, (56)

with r−1r-1 rows and r+d−1r+d-1 columns. By analogy with the Sylvester coefficient matrices used in resultant theory [37], we call (56) the banded Sylvester matrix associated to f0+⋯+fd​zdf_{0}+\cdots+f_{d}z^{d}. We define

Mr=coker⁡Φr.M_{r}=\coker\Phi_{r}.

When 1≤d≤n1\leq d\leq n and f0,…,fdf_{0},\ldots,f_{d} form a regular sequence in SS, the matrix Φr\Phi_{r}, represented by the banded Sylvester matrix (56), satisfies the hypotheses of the Buchsbaum–Rim complex recalled in Appendix A. The resulting resolution is

0⟶Bd+1⟶⋯⟶B2⟶S​(−e)r+d−1→ΦrSr−1⟶Mr⟶0.0\longrightarrow B_{d+1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow B_{2}\longrightarrow S(-e)^{r+d-1}\xrightarrow{\Phi_{r}}S^{r-1}\longrightarrow M_{r}\longrightarrow 0. (57)

The resulting Hilbert series is

HS⁡(Mr;t)=(1−te)d+1(1−t)n+1​∑j=0r−2(r−1−j)​(d+j−1d−1)​te​j.\operatorname{HS}(M_{r};t)=\frac{(1-t^{e})^{d+1}}{(1-t)^{n+1}}\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}(r-1-j)\binom{d+j-1}{d-1}t^{ej}. (58)

Write

Pn​(m)={(m+nn),m≥0,0,m<0.P_{n}(m)=\begin{cases}\binom{m+n}{n},&m\geq 0,\\ 0,&m<0.\end{cases}

Under this regular-sequence hypothesis, for the remaining line bundles

L=𝒪X​(−r,b),r≥2,b≥0,L=\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,b),\qquad r\geq 2,\quad b\geq 0,

the hypersurface long exact sequence gives

and the neighbouring H0H^{0} contribution is

h0​(X,L)res=(r+d−1)​Pn​(b−e)−(r−1)​Pn​(b)+HF⁡(Mr,b).h^{0}(X,L)_{\mathrm{res}}=(r+d-1)P_{n}(b-e)-(r-1)P_{n}(b)+\operatorname{HF}(M_{r},b). (60)

The Serre-dual range is obtained from

KX≃𝒪X​(d−2,e−n−1),K_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{X}(d-2,e-n-1),

and the remaining finite ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-boundary line bundles are computed directly from the same ambient long exact sequence. The formula above agrees with the generating-function formula for ℙ1×ℙn\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{n} hypersurfaces in [35].

The Calabi–Yau threefold

X=[ℙ12ℙ34],X=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}\mathbb{P}^{1}&2\\ \mathbb{P}^{3}&4\end{array}\right],

is a special case of the preceding calculation. Write a line bundle as 𝒪X​(k1,k2)\mathcal{O}_{X}(k_{1},k_{2}), and set

ind⁡(k1,k2)=χ⁡(X,𝒪X​(k1,k2))=13​(6​k1​k22+k23+6​k1+11​k2).\operatorname{ind}(k_{1},k_{2})=\chi(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(k_{1},k_{2}))=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(6k_{1}k_{2}^{2}+k_{2}^{3}+6k_{1}+11k_{2}\bigr).

k1=−r,k2=b,r≥1,b>0.k_{1}=-r,\qquad k_{2}=b,\qquad r\geq 1,\quad b>0.

Fr​(b):=[tb]​(1−t4)3(1−t)4​∑j=0r−2(r−1−j)​(j+1)​t4​j,h1​(X,𝒪X​(−r,b))=Fr​(b),F_{r}(b):=[t^{b}]\frac{(1-t^{4})^{3}}{(1-t)^{4}}\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}(r-1-j)(j+1)t^{4j},\qquad h^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,b))=F_{r}(b), (62)

where the sum is empty for r=1r=1, hence F1​(b)=0F_{1}(b)=0. This agrees with the direct long-exact-sequence computation for 𝒪X​(−1,b)\mathcal{O}_{X}(-1,b). The same sequence gives

h0​(X,𝒪X​(−r,b))=ind⁡(−r,b)+Fr​(b).h^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,b))=\operatorname{ind}(-r,b)+F_{r}(b).

Fr​(b)={−ind⁡(−r,b),0<b<4​r,r+1−ind⁡(−r,4​r),b=4​r,323​r​(r2−1),b>4​r.F_{r}(b)=\begin{cases}-\operatorname{ind}(-r,b),&0<b<4r,\\ r+1-\operatorname{ind}(-r,4r),&b=4r,\\ \dfrac{32}{3}r(r^{2}-1),&b>4r.\end{cases} (63)

After substituting r=−k1r=-k_{1} and b=k2b=k_{2}, this is exactly the wall term in [30]. The remaining chambers either involve no actual map or are obtained from this one by Serre duality, so we do not repeat them here.

3.1.2 The bicubic ℙ2×ℙ2​[3,3]\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}[3,3]

Let

X⊂ℙx2×ℙy2,[X]=(3,3),X\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}_{x}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}_{y},\qquad[X]=(3,3),

and write

f⁡(x,y)=∑|α|=3xα​Fα​(y),Fα∈S3,S=ℂ⁡[y0,y1,y2].f(x,y)=\sum_{|\alpha|=3}x^{\alpha}F_{\alpha}(y),\qquad F_{\alpha}\in S_{3},\qquad S=\mathbb{C}[y_{0},y_{1},y_{2}]. (64)

Consider the chamber

0→𝒪A​(−r−3,b−3)⟶f𝒪A​(−r,b)→L→0.0\to\mathcal{O}_{A}(-r-3,b-3)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{O}_{A}(-r,b)\to L\to 0.

(Φr)β,γ={Fγ−β,γi≥βi​for all ​i,0,otherwise.(\Phi_{r})_{\beta,\gamma}=\begin{cases}F_{\gamma-\beta},&\gamma_{i}\geq\beta_{i}\ \text{for all }i,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (67)

(F300F210F201F120F111F102F030F021F012F003000000F3000F210F2010F120F111F1020F030F021F012F003000F3000F210F2010F120F111F1020F030F021F012F003).\begin{pmatrix}F_{300}&F_{210}&F_{201}&F_{120}&F_{111}&F_{102}&F_{030}&F_{021}&F_{012}&F_{003}&0&0&0&0&0\\ 0&F_{300}&0&F_{210}&F_{201}&0&F_{120}&F_{111}&F_{102}&0&F_{030}&F_{021}&F_{012}&F_{003}&0\\ 0&0&F_{300}&0&F_{210}&F_{201}&0&F_{120}&F_{111}&F_{102}&0&F_{030}&F_{021}&F_{012}&F_{003}\end{pmatrix}.

This finite graded convolution matrix controls the chamber formula: its degree-bb kernel gives h1h^{1}, and its degree-bb cokernel gives h2h^{2}.

Set Mr=coker⁡ΦrM_{r}=\coker\Phi_{r}. We compute the Hilbert function of MrM_{r} by showing that one critical degree map is an isomorphism. For each fixed rr, let Δr​(f)\Delta_{r}(f) be the determinant of

The source and target have the same dimension. To prove that Δr\Delta_{r} is not the zero polynomial in the bicubic coefficients, it is enough to evaluate it at one convenient coefficient point. We choose the special, singular bicubic

f0=(x0​y0+x1​y1+x2​y2)3=∑|α|=3(3α)​xα​yα,f_{0}=(x_{0}y_{0}+x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2})^{3}=\sum_{|\alpha|=3}\binom{3}{\alpha}x^{\alpha}y^{\alpha},

so Fα​(y)=(3α)​yαF_{\alpha}(y)=\binom{3}{\alpha}y^{\alpha}. The singularity of this special member is irrelevant here: it is used only as a nonvanishing certificate for the determinant polynomial.

On the polynomial ring in the xx- and yy-variables define

e=∑i=02xi​∂∂yi,𝖿=∑i=02yi​∂∂xi,h=∑ixi​∂∂xi−∑iyi​∂∂yi.e=\sum_{i=0}^{2}x_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{i}},\qquad\mathsf{f}=\sum_{i=0}^{2}y_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}},\qquad h=\sum_{i}x_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}-\sum_{i}y_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{i}}.

These operators satisfy the 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} relations

[h,e]=2​e,[h,𝖿]=−2​𝖿,[e,𝖿]=h.[h,e]=2e,\qquad[h,\mathsf{f}]=-2\mathsf{f},\qquad[e,\mathsf{f}]=h.

Using divided powers Xγ=xγ/γ!X^{\gamma}=x^{\gamma}/\gamma! in the xx-variables,

𝖿3​(Xγ​yδ)=∑α≤γ|α|=3(3α)​Xγ−α​yδ+α.\mathsf{f}^{3}(X^{\gamma}y^{\delta})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\leq\gamma\\ |\alpha|=3\end{subarray}}\binom{3}{\alpha}X^{\gamma-\alpha}y^{\delta+\alpha}.

This is exactly the degree-rr matrix (Φr)r(\Phi_{r})_{r} for f0f_{0}, up to diagonal rescaling of bases. Indeed |γ|=r|\gamma|=r, |δ|=r−3|\delta|=r-3, β=γ−α\beta=\gamma-\alpha, and the target monomial has degrees |β|=r−3|\beta|=r-3, |δ+α|=r|\delta+\alpha|=r.

Inside the total-degree 2​r−32r-3 subspace, the source Symxr⊗Symyr−3\operatorname{Sym}^{r}_{x}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{r-3}_{y} is the hh-weight 33 subspace, and the target Symxr−3⊗Symyr\operatorname{Sym}^{r-3}_{x}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{r}_{y} is the hh-weight −3-3 subspace. Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, in any finite-dimensional 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}-representation, 𝖿3\mathsf{f}^{3} is an isomorphism between the weight-33 and weight-−3-3 spaces in each irreducible summand: every irreducible summand which contains weight 33 also contains weight −3-3, and the three lowering steps between them have nonzero coefficients. Therefore

Δr​(f0)≠0.\Delta_{r}(f_{0})\neq 0.

It follows that Δr\Delta_{r} is not identically zero. For each fixed rr, the condition Δr​(f)≠0\Delta_{r}(f)\neq 0 defines a nonempty Zariski open subset of the bicubic coefficient space. Intersecting with the smooth locus, for this fixed rr, a general smooth bicubic has (Φr)r(\Phi_{r})_{r} an isomorphism. For a statement uniform in all r≥3r\geq 3, the correct statement is that it holds for a very general smooth bicubic.

Assume now that (Φr)r(\Phi_{r})_{r} is an isomorphism. If b<rb<r and v∈ker⁡(Φr)bv\in\ker(\Phi_{r})_{b}, choose a nonzero u∈Sr−bu\in S_{r-b}. Since Φr\Phi_{r} is an SS-module map,

(Φr)r​(u​v)=u​(Φr)b​(v)=0.(\Phi_{r})_{r}(uv)=u(\Phi_{r})_{b}(v)=0.

The degree-rr map is injective and the source is free, so u​v=0uv=0; hence v=0v=0. Thus (Φr)b(\Phi_{r})_{b} is injective for b<rb<r. Since MrM_{r} is generated by the degree-zero generators coming from the target and (Mr)r=0(M_{r})_{r}=0, all higher pieces vanish:

(Mr)b=Sb−r​(Mr)r=0,b≥r.(M_{r})_{b}=S_{b-r}(M_{r})_{r}=0,\qquad b\geq r.

Thus (Φr)b(\Phi_{r})_{b} is surjective for b≥rb\geq r.

h1​(X,𝒪X​(−r,k2,k3,k4))\displaystyle h^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})) =Fr​(k2,k3,k4),\displaystyle=F_{r}(k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}),
h0​(X,𝒪X​(−r,k2,k3,k4))\displaystyle h^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(-r,k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})) =(r+1)​∏j=24(kj−1)−(r−1)​∏j=24(kj+1)+Fr​(k2,k3,k4).\displaystyle=(r+1)\prod_{j=2}^{4}(k_{j}-1)-(r-1)\prod_{j=2}^{4}(k_{j}+1)+F_{r}(k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}).

This is exactly the stable one-negative tetraquadric formula of [30], after permuting the four ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-factors if necessary: their h1h^{1} is the same FrF_{r}, and their h0h^{0} is the same ambient Euler difference plus FrF_{r}. The boundary k1=0k_{1}=0 is also completely explicit. For b,c,d≥0b,c,d\geq 0,

h0​(X,𝒪X​(0,b,c,d))=(b+1)​(c+1)​(d+1)+u⁡(b−2)​u​(c−2)​u​(d−2),u⁡(m)=max⁡{m+1,0}.h^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(0,b,c,d))=(b+1)(c+1)(d+1)+u(b-2)u(c-2)u(d-2),\qquad u(m)=\max\{m+1,0\}.

Permuting the four factors gives the other one-negative and boundary pieces. Thus, up to permutations and Serre duality, the stable two-negative chamber is the only remaining tetraquadric chamber with a nontrivial active map.

3.2 Codimension-two examples

In this section, we study the examples in [31] and we can see our method can recover all of their formulae analytically.

4 New structures and new formulas from Hilbert functions

In this section we use Hilbert functions in two ways. First, we show that they can detect new structures in line bundle cohomology which are invisible to polynomial extrapolation or machine-learning fits on bounded data. Second, we show that the same Hilbert-function viewpoint can produce analytic cohomology formulae on regions of the Picard lattice, and can reduce the remaining cases to explicit finite-rank or finite-box verification. In either case, we can get cohomology formula for infinitely many line bundles.

4.1 New structures from Hilbert functions

We give three examples in which the ambient cohomology and the source–target dimensions suggest a clean maximal-rank answer, but the Hilbert numerator contains extra terms. These terms produce additional walls inside a fixed ambient-cohomology region. The first two examples come from CICY 78807880: a one-sided top-ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} wall and a finite kernel calculation on the negative-ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} branch. The third example is a bigraded boundary wall in the two-negative region of the tetraquadric 78627862.

4.1.1 CICY 78807880: hidden top-ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} subwalls

We now return to the hypersurface

X7880⊂ℙx1×ℙy1×ℙz2,[X7880]=(2,2,3).X_{7880}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}_{y}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}_{z},\qquad[X_{7880}]=(2,2,3).

Write the defining equation as

4.2 New formulae: CICY 77077707 as a case study

This subsection gives a complete worked example of the method on CICY 77077707. The goal is to show how Hilbert-function calculations can be used to derive new line-bundle cohomology formulae for a CICY that was not previously covered by a closed formula package. In practice the output has two complementary parts. Some chambers admit uniform analytic Hilbert-series arguments, while other chambers are controlled by finite-box theorems proved by exact computational commutative algebra. The latter can still cover a large and useful class of line bundles. Let

X7707=[ℙx111ℙy102ℙz331],X_{7707}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|cc}\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}&1&1\\ \mathbb{P}^{1}_{y}&0&2\\ \mathbb{P}^{3}_{z}&3&1\end{array}\right],

and put

Write

F=x0​A0​(z)+x1​A1​(z),G=x0​B0​(y,z)+x1​B1​(y,z),F=x_{0}A_{0}(z)+x_{1}A_{1}(z),\qquad G=x_{0}B_{0}(y,z)+x_{1}B_{1}(y,z), (82)

where

Ai∈H0​(ℙz3,𝒪⁡(3)),Bi∈H0​(ℙy1×ℙz3,𝒪⁡(2,1)).A_{i}\in H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{3}_{z},\mathcal{O}(3)),\qquad B_{i}\in H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{y}\times\mathbb{P}^{3}_{z},\mathcal{O}(2,1)).

Eliminating the ℙx1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{x}-coordinate gives

The formulae above cover the ranges with nontrivial active maps. The remaining boundary cases, the possible d2d_{2}-maps, and the compatibility of the finite-field verifications on a common open set introduce no new formula mechanism; we collect them in Appendix D.

It is negative for 0≤m<b−40\leq m<b-4 and positive for m>b−4m>b-4; for b=4b=4 the negative side is empty and the zero lies on the boundary of the ray. More explicitly, the finite-box formula can be read as

h∙​(X,𝒪X​(−m−4,b))={(0,−E⁡(m,b),0,0),0≤m<b−4,(0,0,0,0),m=b−4,(0,0,E⁡(m,b),0),b−4<m<6​b−4,(0,0,4​b​(14​b2−11)3,Nb​(m)),m≥6​b−4.h^{\bullet}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}(-m-4,b))=\begin{cases}(0,-E(m,b),0,0),&0\leq m<b-4,\\ (0,0,0,0),&m=b-4,\\ (0,0,E(m,b),0),&b-4<m<6b-4,\\ \left(0,0,\dfrac{4b(14b^{2}-11)}{3},N_{b}(m)\right),&m\geq 6b-4.\end{cases}

In the last line we used the identity

which follows by substituting the numerator (93). Hence the finite box contains two structural walls: the Euler wall a=−ba=-b, where the middle cohomology switches from h1h^{1} to h2h^{2}, and the hidden endpoint wall a=−6​ba=-6b, where h3=Nb​(m)h^{3}=N_{b}(m) turns on. Cell 7373 is obtained from Theorem 8 by Serre duality.

5 Conclusions and future directions

The main point of this paper is that chamber formulae for CICY line-bundle cohomology have a concrete algebraic source. Once the Koszul spectral sequence is written in explicit bases, the non-trivial maps become multiplication maps between ambient cohomology groups, and their rank defects are measured by Hilbert functions of cokernel or kernel modules. This turns many previously empirical chamber formulae into explicit rank-defect statements: in some chambers the relevant graded modules admit analytic Hilbert-series computations, while in others the ranks are fixed by finite-box certificates.

We have developed this viewpoint through a range of examples. In the cases where formulae were already available in the literature, the Hilbert-function description recovers many of them from a uniform algebraic mechanism. In other examples, the same method reveals refined wall and subwall structures which are not visible from ambient cohomology regions or from polynomial fitting on finite data. These structures are not introduced as additional ansatzes; they arise from the same endpoint modules, cokernel modules, and kernel modules that control the Koszul ranks.

The method also produces new line-bundle cohomology formulae for CICY examples which had not previously been treated by closed-form formula libraries. Some of these formulae follow from analytic Hilbert-series arguments, while others are obtained as finite-box formulae in regions where a uniform analytic resolution is not yet available. In both situations, the essential object is the Hilbert function attached to the non-trivial Koszul map, rather than the individual finite-dimensional rank computation for each line bundle.

The computational consequence is direct. A certified formula replaces large Koszul matrix construction and rank computation by coefficient extraction from a Hilbert series, by a closed expression, or by a replayable finite certificate. Thus even a partial formula library is useful for scans: every certified chamber removes an infinite family, or a specified finite region, of matrix-rank computations from future line-bundle calculations. The results of this paper therefore suggest that Hilbert functions are natural objects to study in the construction of line-bundle cohomology formula libraries for CICYs and related Calabi–Yau geometries.

Several natural directions follow from the method of this paper. First, it would be useful to build machine-readable CICY line-bundle cohomology libraries along these lines, even if many entries are finite-box theorems rather than global chamber formulae. Second, one should adapt the method to toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, where Cox rings are intrinsic and line-bundle cohomology is again governed by graded pieces of Koszul-type maps, but where the chamber structure, irrelevant ideals, and saturation issues are richer. Third, it would be interesting to incorporate freely acting quotients: equivariant Koszul maps should lead to representation-valued versions of the same Hilbert-function calculation, allowing invariant cohomology downstairs to be computed from equivariant data upstairs. Such CICY and toric Calabi–Yau cohomology libraries, together with their quotient versions, would provide faster and more transparent input for string model-building searches based on line-bundle constructions. Finally, it remains an interesting question whether each CICY admits line-bundle cohomology generating functions in the sense of [35]. This direction has its own mathematical interest, independently of the finite-box formulae emphasized here.

Appendix A General algebraic tools

Buchsbaum–Rim exactness.

All polynomial rings in this appendix are over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Whenever a sequence of forms is assumed to be regular, the corresponding statement applies to a sufficiently general choice of the defining equations used in the main text.

Let

ϕ:F⟶G\phi:F\longrightarrow G

be a homogeneous map of free modules over a polynomial ring RR, with

rank⁡F=f,rank⁡G=g,f≥g,\operatorname{rank}F=f,\qquad\operatorname{rank}G=g,\qquad f\geq g,

and put M=coker⁡ϕM=\operatorname{coker}\phi. Let Ig​(ϕ)⊂RI_{g}(\phi)\subset R be the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a matrix for ϕ\phi. The closed subscheme defined by Ig​(ϕ)I_{g}(\phi) is the maximal-rank degeneracy locus of ϕ\phi; set-theoretically, it is the locus where ϕ\phi fails to have rank gg. Its expected codimension is f−g+1f-g+1.

Write p=f−gp=f-g. The Buchsbaum–Rim complex resolving MM, when it is exact, has the form

0→Cp+1→Cp→⋯→C2→F⟶ϕG→M→0,0\to C_{p+1}\to C_{p}\to\cdots\to C_{2}\to F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}G\to M\to 0, (95)

with

Ci+1=⋀g+iF⊗Symi−1⁡(G∨)⊗⋀gG∨,1≤i≤p.C_{i+1}=\bigwedge^{g+i}F\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{i-1}(G^{\vee})\otimes\bigwedge^{g}G^{\vee},\qquad 1\leq i\leq p. (96)

We do not need explicit formulas for the differentials; for Hilbert-series computations the free modules in (96) suffice.

The Buchsbaum–Rim exactness criterion [38, 39] states:

If grade⁡Ig​(ϕ)≥f−g+1\operatorname{grade}I_{g}(\phi)\geq f-g+1, then the Buchsbaum–Rim complex is exact and gives a free resolution of coker⁡ϕ\operatorname{coker}\phi.

Since RR is a polynomial ring, this is equivalent in our applications to showing that Ig​(ϕ)I_{g}(\phi) has height f−g+1f-g+1. By the determinantal height bound, this is the expected and maximal possible height. In the applications below we verify this height condition by identifying the degeneracy locus, up to radical, with the zero locus of an explicit regular sequence. Once this condition is verified, the Hilbert numerator of coker⁡ϕ\operatorname{coker}\phi is obtained directly from the alternating sum of the free modules in the Buchsbaum–Rim resolution.

We now apply this criterion to the Toeplitz-type maps that arise in our Koszul computations. Assume r≥2r\geq 2 and d≥1d\geq 1. Let S=ℂ⁡[y0,…,yn]S=\mathbb{C}[y_{0},\dots,y_{n}] and consider the map

Φr:S​(−e)r+d−1⟶Sr−1,\Phi_{r}:S(-e)^{r+d-1}\longrightarrow S^{r-1},

where the matrix has the Toeplitz form determined by coefficients f0,…,fd∈Sef_{0},\dots,f_{d}\in S_{e}. The target rank is g=r−1g=r-1, the source rank is f=r+d−1f=r+d-1; hence

f−g+1=d+1.f-g+1=d+1.

We must therefore check that the locus where Φr\Phi_{r} fails to have rank r−1r-1 has codimension d+1d+1.

Evaluate the coefficients f0,…,fdf_{0},\dots,f_{d} at a point, obtaining numbers a0,…,ada_{0},\dots,a_{d}. The rows of the resulting numerical matrix are the coefficient vectors of

F⁡(z),z​F​(z),…,zr−2​F​(z),F⁡(z)=a0+a1​z+⋯+ad​zd.F(z),\ zF(z),\ \dots,\ z^{r-2}F(z),\qquad F(z)=a_{0}+a_{1}z+\cdots+a_{d}z^{d}.

If these rows had a linear relation, then for some scalars c0,…,cr−2c_{0},\dots,c_{r-2} we would have

(c0+c1​z+⋯+cr−2​zr−2)​F​(z)=0.\bigl(c_{0}+c_{1}z+\cdots+c_{r-2}z^{r-2}\bigr)F(z)=0.

When F≠0F\neq 0, this forces c0+⋯+cr−2​zr−2=0c_{0}+\cdots+c_{r-2}z^{r-2}=0, hence all ci=0c_{i}=0. Thus the rows are linearly independent whenever F≠0F\neq 0. Equivalently, the rank drops at a point if and only if

If f0,…,fdf_{0},\dots,f_{d} form a regular sequence, this ideal has height d+1=f−g+1d+1=f-g+1. Therefore the Buchsbaum–Rim criterion applies.

In the Toeplitz case, the exact complex is

0→Bd+1→Bd→⋯→B2→S​(−e)r+d−1⟶ΦrSr−1→Mr→0,0\to B_{d+1}\to B_{d}\to\cdots\to B_{2}\to S(-e)^{r+d-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi_{r}}}{{\longrightarrow}}S^{r-1}\to M_{r}\to 0, (97)

The finite black-line statements for 78337833 and 78837883 use the same nonzero-minor principle. The companion repository https://github.com/jtwangbimsa-dragon/cicylinecoh_alpha stores replay data organized by CICY number. Each entry contains a deterministic specialization, a prime field, and pivot/minor data for a specific full-rank minor. The verifier rebuilds the corresponding integer matrix, reduces it modulo the specified prime, and replays the pivot/minor check. A successful replay proves that the same integer minor is nonzero, so the rank condition holds over ℚ\mathbb{Q} and on a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the complex coefficient space.

For 78447844, the archive contains the right-endpoint checks for 3≤r≤153\leq r\leq 15 and 0≤b≤Br+10\leq b\leq B_{r}+1 described above. For 78337833, it contains 4646 right-endpoint checks on

(r,b)=(3​q,2​q),2≤q≤23,(r,b)=(3q,2q),\qquad 2\leq q\leq 23,

three bottom layers for each qq.

For 78337833 and 78837883, the verifier exploits the special structure of the endpoint matrices to reduce the amount of stored pivot data.

After the endpoint ranks are replayed, they are used exactly as in the main text. For 78337833, the verified right endpoint vanishes on the two listed black lines, while the left endpoint vanishes there by the shifted endpoint numerator. For 78837883, the left endpoint vanishes on (r,b)=(3​q,2​q)(r,b)=(3q,2q), the right endpoint has dimension 11 at q=1q=1, and vanishes for 2≤q≤232\leq q\leq 23. In every case, the remaining middle cohomology entry is then determined by the row Euler characteristic.

Lemma 2.

Assume that

Θp,q​(R):SR−3a→SRb\Theta_{p,q}(R):S_{R-3}^{a}\to S_{R}^{b}

is injective and that

Θp,q​(R+1):SR−2a→SR+1b\Theta_{p,q}(R+1):S_{R-2}^{a}\to S_{R+1}^{b}

is surjective. Then Θp,q​(c)\Theta_{p,q}(c) has maximal rank for every c≥0c\geq 0. Equivalently,

HF⁡(Mp,q,c)=max⁡{b​(c+22)−a​(c−12),0}\operatorname{HF}(M_{p,q},c)=\max\left\{b\binom{c+2}{2}-a\binom{c-1}{2},0\right\}

for all cc, with the convention (c−12)=0\binom{c-1}{2}=0 for c<3c<3.

Proof.

If c<Rc<R, any nonzero kernel vector in degree cc can be multiplied by a nonzero form of degree R−cR-c. Since SS is a domain and the source is free, this gives a nonzero kernel vector in degree RR, contradicting the assumed injectivity there. Hence all maps in degrees c≤Rc\leq R are injective.

For c≥R+1c\geq R+1, surjectivity in degree R+1R+1 is the statement (Mp,q)R+1=0(M_{p,q})_{R+1}=0. Since Mp,qM_{p,q} is a quotient of SbS^{b}, it is generated in degree 00, and each higher graded piece is obtained by multiplying the previous ones by linear forms. Therefore (Mp,q)c=0(M_{p,q})_{c}=0 for every c≥R+1c\geq R+1, so all maps in these degrees are surjective. This gives maximal rank in every degree, and the displayed Hilbert function is the target dimension minus the rank. ∎

The pivot certificates are characteristic-zero certificates, not merely finite-field evidence. After deterministic integer coefficients are chosen for the cubics Fα​βF_{\alpha\beta}, the two critical maps become integer matrices. If sparse elimination modulo a prime ℓ\ell finds a minor of the required size which is nonzero in 𝔽ℓ\mathbb{F}_{\ell}, then that minor is a nonzero integer, so the same rank statement holds over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Equivalently, this minor is a nonzero polynomial condition on the coefficients of the Fα​βF_{\alpha\beta}, and hence holds on a nonempty Zariski-open subset. Intersecting the finitely many certified open conditions with the smoothness open gives the claimed generic statement.

Therefore, for every fixed (p,q)(p,q) with certificates at RR and R+1R+1, Lemma 2 proves the positive-part Hilbert function for all cc. The certificates for

2≤p,q≤142\leq p,q\leq 14

cover 169169 infinite cc-rays in the top-ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} chamber of CICY 78807880, not merely 169169 isolated line bundles. This statement has two important limits. First, it is a generic statement: special complex structures may have lower ranks and hence larger cohomology. Second, it is a statement in the full coefficient space of the hypersurface. If one restricts to an invariant or symmetric subfamily of defining polynomials, the same minor-nonvanishing argument must be repeated inside that smaller coefficient space.

The accompanying endpoint certificates replay this quotient-rank calculation: for each b=4,…,10b=4,\ldots,10, they rebuild the relevant matrices over 𝔽1000003\mathbb{F}_{1000003}, check the stored hashes, leading terms, reduction identities, and pivot minors, and recover the numerator in (109).

The next input is the left end of the reduced Koszul complex. For every b=4,…,10b=4,\ldots,10, the reduced leftmost map corresponding to

d3:C3⟶C2d_{3}:C_{3}\longrightarrow C_{2}

has a full-column-rank certificate. The certificate lists pivot rows for a square minor using all columns and checks that its determinant is nonzero modulo 10000031000003. Hence the leftmost map is injective on the certified open set.

For each b=4,…,10b=4,\ldots,10, we rebuild all relevant matrix blocks in the reduced Koszul complex, compute their exact ranks, verify that adjacent compositions vanish, and then compute the middle homology directly from dimH=dimker−dimim\dim H=\dim\ker-\dim\operatorname{im}. The result is that no simultaneous middle correction remains, and

ℋ3=0,ℋ0=Nb,ℋ1=[E+Nb]+,ℋ2=[−E−Nb]+.\mathcal{H}_{3}=0,\qquad\mathcal{H}_{0}=N_{b},\qquad\mathcal{H}_{1}=[E+N_{b}]_{+},\qquad\mathcal{H}_{2}=[-E-N_{b}]_{+}.

All matrices above have entries in the integer polynomial ring generated by the coefficients of Q,L1,L2Q,L_{1},L_{2}. A pivot minor or standard-basis leading coefficient which is nonzero modulo 10000031000003 is the reduction of a nonzero integer polynomial in those coefficients. Thus each recorded rank or initial-module condition defines a nonempty Zariski-open condition in characteristic zero. Intersecting the finitely many opens from the endpoint numerator, left injectivity, and middle-rank certificates with the smoothness open for the complete intersection gives the general smooth member claimed in Theorem 8. Cell 7373 follows by Calabi–Yau Serre duality.
